papers.title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
papers.abstract: Legged locomotion on flowing ground ({\em e.g.} granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s ($\approx 60$ cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction $\phi$ and the limb frequency $\omega$, and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when $\phi$ becomes small enough and/or $\omega$ large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.

papers.title: Functional understanding of structural components in polypseudorotaxane gels
papers.abstract: Biomedical devices, wearable interfaces, and soft robots require compliant soft materials with reliable mechanical performance, yet the molecular principles needed to design such materials are not always fully understood. Thus, there is an urgent need to understand how to design novel stretchable and soft hydrogels with enhanced toughness, i.e. resistance to breakage. Slide-ring gels (SRGs) are a class of unconventional soft materials formed by polyrotaxanes (PR) building blocks whereby sliding cyclodextrins (CD) replace traditional chemical and physical crosslinks and in turn enhance toughness and stretchability by several orders of magnitude. The rational design of SRGs re- mains challenging due to a lack of a mechanistic understanding of the role played by individual components. In this work, we implement simple synthetic perturbations that individually target polymer-CD and CD-CD interactions in unstoppered pseudopolyrotaxanes (pPR) solutions and measure the consequent changes in viscoelastic properties. Weakening the intermolecular interaction between CDs abolishes crystallisation and significantly weakens the gel. At the same time, thermodynamically favouring threading by using azobenzene-modified PEG chains favours the formation of stable and long-lived networks even at remarkably low CD stoichiometries. We rationalise these observations with coarse-grained Molecular Dynamics simulations which clarify the structure-function relationship of the components forming these materials. Our work contributes to guiding the rational design and development of enhanced SRG hydrogels and elastomers.

papers.title: Non-Destructive Detection of Early Drought Stress via Spectral Submanifold Analysis
papers.abstract: Non-destructive early detection of water stress is critical for precision agriculture, yet current detection methods are often labor-intensive or destructive. We propose a rapid, non-invasive method based on Spectral Submanifold (SSM) reduction to analyze the nonlinear vibration dynamics of soybean plants. Unlike traditional linear modal analysis, our data-driven approach reveals a distinct transition in the dominant dynamics of the plant stem as drought progresses. Specifically, we uncover a sign reversal in the nonlinear damping coefficient within SSM-reduced models of full plants. Our finding reveals a fundamental transition in the plant's dissipative mechanics from a pressurized, fluid-rich vessel exhibiting superlinear (viscoelastic) damping to a dry, cellular solid dominated by sublinear (frictional) damping. This transition is closely correlated with the onset of physiological stress indicated by a significant decrease in the values of mature-leaf soil plant analysis development (SPAD) and colorimetric metrics. In contrast, traditional metrics, such as linear frequency and leaf wilting, do not provide consistent statistical signals of water stress. This study provides the first experimental evidence that SSM-based nonlinear model reduction can detect the changing internal state of a living organism, offering a physics-based metric for high-throughput plant phenotyping.

papers.title: Shear-induced mechanical yielding controls cluster morphology and dynamics in aggregating non-Brownian suspensions
papers.abstract: In sheared aggregating suspensions, flow drives both the formation and breakage of particle clusters, whose dynamic evolution influences transport and rheological properties. Understanding these mechanisms remains challenging due to the complex interplay between interparticle forces, hydrodynamic interactions, and shear flow. Using parallelized Accelerated Stokesian Dynamics (PASD) simulations, we investigate cluster microstructure and rotational dynamics, and how their coupling produces suspension stress in sheared, attractive non-Brownian suspensions. When interparticle attraction dominates over separating shear forces, clusters grow until mechanical loading balances maximum interparticle bond strength. We examine how the cluster stresslet depends on cluster size, with both quantities normalized by their mechanical yielding scales. Scaled cluster stresslets collapse onto a master curve exhibiting three distinct regimes: cubic, quadratic, and linear with respect to the scaled radius of gyration $R_g$. In the cubic regime, small, compact clusters behave as rigid bodies, whose hydrodynamic stresslet scales with cluster volume $R_g^3$. As clusters grow into the quadratic regime, low-aspect-ratio clusters preferentially yield under flow, driving a proportional increase in average aspect ratio with size. High-aspect-ratio clusters follow Jeffery rotational dynamics within the flow-gradient plane, spending longer durations aligned with the flow and thereby reducing their time-averaged hydrodynamic stresslet to scale as $R_g^2$. In the linear regime, clusters approach the maximum size sustainable by the interparticle bonds. The internal tension is bounded by the maximum bond strength, limiting the stresslet to an $R_g$ dependence. These findings establish a mechanistic framework connecting microscale cluster morphology and dynamics to macroscale rheology.

papers.title: Emergent Entropic Forces Drive Inverse and Reentrant Phase Transitions in Condensates of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
papers.abstract: We present a phenomenological, mean-field model for condensates of intrinsically disordered proteins that describes inverse phase transitions and qualitatively predicts reentrant phase behavior as a function of salt concentration. The model is based on a matrix-based formulation of the Flory-Huggins free energy, in which the enthalpic interaction parameter and the protein valence, defined here as the number of effective "sticky patches", are treated as free parameters. Its central insight is that integrating out dynamics of fast-moving molecular species generates an effective entropic force that increases the free-energy barrier to mixing, even within a mean-field description. We account for this by linking Gaussian integration of co-solutes to the Schur complement of the matrix-based Flory-Huggins free energy. This provides a general thermodynamic framework illustrating how enthalpic interactions that increase the number of available microstates necessarily induce effective entropic forces. We demonstrate the expressiveness and predictive power of the model by qualitatively reproducing recent experimental observations on the rabies virus phosphoprotein.

papers.title: Strain Waves Generate Compression and Trigger Buckling in Active Polymers
papers.abstract: Chemical reactions can sustain polymer motion without necessarily generating the compression required for buckling. Theory and simulations show that tension-dependent chemical transitions coupled to bond elasticity generate finite-wavelength traveling strain waves in a semiflexible polymer. In the straight chain at fixed axial span, the waves reduce mean active contraction while leaving mean elastic tension unchanged, generating compression that drives bending above a threshold. Releasing the mean load allows longitudinal waves to persist while transverse perturbations decay.

papers.title: Surface morphology and shear effect on lubricated granular system
papers.abstract: Improving the particle surface frictional behavior is of considerable importance in several industries so as to manipulate the powder flowability and handling. In this work, we have studied the lubrication phenomena in an assembly of flowing bulk powder particles in presence of a fine powder lubricant. Experiments were conducted in two different shear environments, for two different levels of confinement and using three different bulk powder particles having distinct surface morphology. The added lubricant particles tend to adhere to the surface of bulk particles thereby altering their surface morphology. This results in altered inter-particle friction, which typically reduces for small addition of lubricant, but increases on its excess addition, thereby altering the particle flowability. While this behavior is generally understood through previous studies, the current work explores how the effect of confinement, shear environment and particle surface characteristics combine in a unique manner to provide modified flow behavior for different lubricant concentrations. Extended shear duration seems to extend the range of lubricant concentrations for improved flowability. On the other hand flow confinement seems to limit the extent of lubrication for these range of concentrations. Both these opposing effects also exhibit a unique dependence on the particle surface morphology and its seeming affinity with the lubricant particle. The parameter types and ranges explored comprise most conditions encountered in industrial systems, the outcome thereby providing a basis for designing of applications handling lubricant-particle mixtures.

papers.title: Active phase separation from concentration-dependent diffusion in chemical networks
papers.abstract: Active phase separation in living systems is ubiquitous, yet the microscopic origins of the non-equilibrium terms in active field theories remain largely unknown. Here, starting from stochastic mass-conserving reaction-diffusion dynamics of two interacting chemical species, we perform a systematic slow-mode reduction and derive the complete Active Model B+ field theory, with all phenomenological coefficients expressed in terms of microscopic parameters. We identify concentration-dependent diffusivities and asymmetric inter-species chemotactic couplings as the minimal microscopic ingredients generating the genuinely non-equilibrium coefficient responsible for microphase separation, cluster phases, and arrested coarsening. Our framework recovers the equilibrium limit consistently and is validated by stochastic numerical simulations. These results establish a direct, bottom-up link between the architecture of chemical reaction networks and the universality class of their emergent large-scale dynamics.

papers.title: Entropy-production cost limits hierarchical decision-making in homing pigeon flocks
papers.abstract: Collective decision-making requires individuals to reconcile diverse, often conflicting opinions to reach a common course of action. However, within a group, they rarely exert equal influence, leading to non-reciprocal communication patterns manifested as leader-follower relationships and social hierarchies. Here, using homing pigeon flocks as a model system, we develop a trajectory-based framework to infer and quantify hierarchy within navigating living collectives. We find that while small flocks exhibit pronounced hierarchy, increasing flock size progressively weakens it, driving the collection toward more egalitarian decision-making. We provide a physical basis of this observation using a thermodynamic framework in which non-reciprocal communication between birds carries an information-entropy cost. Our calculations reveal that hierarchy weakening observed in larger flocks is a direct consequence of maintaining a constant per-individual entropy production rate across flock sizes. Together, these results suggest that constraints on information-processing capacity may play an important role in the collective dynamics of living organisms.

papers.title: Supercoiling Drives DNA-Protein Co-Condensation
papers.abstract: The co-condensation of DNA and proteins plays an important role in genome compaction, including heterochromatin formation and chromosome segregation. Meanwhile, transcription and replication continuously generate DNA supercoiling, yet how the resulting torsional stress affects co-condensation remains poorly understood. Here, by coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, we show that supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for co-condensation through a mutually reinforcing interplay with protein wetting. Specifically, protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, generating highly writhed DNA conformations that in turn promote capillary collapse into a protein-rich droplet. In the absence of supercoiling, DNA remains kinetically trapped in metastable extended states within our model, whereas sufficiently strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation. These results establish topology as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation and provide a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes can dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

papers.title: On buoyancy in disperse two-phase flow and its impact on the well-posedness of two-fluid models
papers.abstract: The Maxey--Riley--Gatignol equation for the flow around a sphere at low particle Reynolds number tells us that the fluid-particle interaction force decomposes into a contribution from the local flow disturbance caused by the particle's boundary---consisting of the drag, virtual-mass, and history forces, and their Fax\'en corrections---and another contribution from the stress of the background flow, termed generalized-buoyancy force. There is also a consensus that, for general disperse two-phase flow, the interfacial force density, coupling the average fluid phase and dispersed-phase momentum balances, decomposes in a like manner. However, there has been a long-standing controversy about the physical closure separating the generalized-buoyancy from the interfacial force density, especially whether or not pseudo-stresses, such as the Reynolds stress, should be attributed to the background flow. Furthermore, most existing propositions for this closure involve small-particle approximations. Here, we show that all existing buoyancy closures are inconsistent with particle-resolving numerical simulations and/or at least one of two simple thought experiments designed to determine the roles of pseudo-stresses and small-particle approximations. We then derive the unique consistent closure. It requires no approximation and implies that all stresses and pseudo-stresses in the average fluid phase momentum balance, except the Reynolds stress, fully contribute to the background flow responsible for buoyancy. Remarkably, it exhibits a low-pass filter property, attenuating buoyancy at short wavelengths, that prevents it from causing Hadamard instabilities, constituting a first-principles-based solution to the long-standing ill-posedness problem of two-fluid models. When employing the derived closure, even simplistic two-fluid models are linearly well-posed.

papers.title: Directional Control of Droplet Motion via Geometric Gating
papers.abstract: We explore new methods for inducing the movement of water droplets on elastomeric substrates, such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Our approach builds upon the well-known phenomenon that water droplets move easily across these substrates when swelled w,ith silicone oil. While designing shallow open channels and traps on a PDMS film offers a simple way to control a droplet's trajectory by tilting the substrate in two orthogonal directions, this method is poorly suited for manipulating multiple droplets simultaneously. To address this limitation, we introduce two new methods. The first method utilizes a plano-concave PDMS platform with a radius of curvature significantly larger than the size of the droplet and its translation distance. When the system's configuration is altered, this curved substrate consistently guides the droplet along a curved geodesic. The second method incorporates diode-like gates on the PDMS. These gates are created on either flat or plano-concave PDMS films by embedding thin, rigid plates into the elastomer prior to crosslinking, followed by swelling in silicone oil. This process generates sigmoidal steps that restrict droplet motion to a single direction. Finally, we demonstrate how combining these two strategies enables various forms of directed motion for both single and multiple droplets.

papers.title: Mobility, response and transport in non-equilibrium coarse-grained models
papers.abstract: We investigate two different types of non-Markovian coarse-grained models extracted from a linear, non-equilibrium microscopic system, featuring a tagged particle coupled to underdamped oscillators. The first model is obtained by analytically ``integrating out'' the oscillators and the second is based on a derivation using projection operator techniques. We observe that these two models behave very differently when the tagged particle is exposed to external harmonic potentials or pulling forces. Most importantly, we find that the analytic model has a well defined friction kernel and can be used to extract work, consistent with the microscopic system, while the projection model corresponds to an effective equilibrium model, which cannot be used to extract work. We apply the analysis to two popular non-equilibrium systems, time-delay feedback control and the active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Finally, we highlight that our study could have important consequences for dynamic coarse-graining of non-equilibrium systems going far beyond the linear systems investigated in this manuscript.

papers.title: Universal winding laws in chiral active motion
papers.abstract: Chiral active particles, from bacteria and sperm cells to engineered microswimmers, undergo persistent motion that breaks both time-reversal and mirror symmetries. This broken mirror symmetry leaves geometric signatures in trajectories that cannot be captured by conventional measures like position fluctuations. Here we identify the signed area and winding angle as key observables to characterize the geometric and topological aspects of the trajectories of chiral active particles. Combining theory, experiment, and computer simulations, we demonstrate that these observables exhibit universal growth laws and fluctuation statistics that are independent of propulsion details. The presence of chirality generates multiple off-centred closed loops in the trajectories, resulting in a linear temporal growth of the signed area and a much slower logarithmic growth for the winding angle. Our work uncovers universal trajectory-level signatures of chirality and provides a unifying description of chiral dynamics in active matter.
